decks.title: Chemistry in Everyday Life — Part 1: Chemicals in medicines
goals: Explain how drugs act on targets such as enzymes and receptors
Classify drugs by pharmacological effect and give examples
Describe antacids, antihistamines, tranquilisers, analgesics, antimicrobials and antifertility drugs
Distinguish antiseptics from disinfectants and bactericidal from bacteriostatic antibiotics

slides.heading: Chemistry in Everyday Life
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how medicines work, chemically. (Formative assessment only; not in the board exam.)

visual.alt: Table of everyday situations and the types of drug used

slides.narration: Namaste! Medicines are chemicals that interact with molecules in our bodies. Every time you take a tablet for acidity, a cold or a headache, a chemical reaction is going on inside you. In this part we look at how drugs act and at the main classes of medicine. This chapter is assessed in school, not in the board exam. Remember: medicines must only be taken as a doctor advises.

slides.heading: Drugs and medicines
slides.body_md: **Drugs** are chemicals of low molecular mass (about 100–500 u) that interact with macromolecular targets in the body and produce a biological response. When the response is **therapeutic** and useful, they are **medicines**, used to diagnose, prevent or treat disease. Most drugs are harmful at higher doses, so they are used only under medical supervision.

rows: Drugs acting on enzymes or receptors

visual.alt: Table of the bases for classifying drugs with examples

slides.narration: A drug is a fairly small molecule that interacts with large molecules in the body, such as proteins, and changes how they work. If the effect is useful in treating or preventing disease, the drug is called a medicine. The same substance can heal at one dose and harm at another, which is why medicines are taken only as prescribed. Drugs can be classified by their effect, their action, their structure or their target.

slides.heading: Drugs that act on enzymes
slides.body_md: Enzymes hold their **substrate** in an **active site**. A drug that is similar in shape to the substrate can occupy the active site instead: a **competitive inhibitor**. Some drugs bind elsewhere (an **allosteric site**) and change the shape of the active site. If the bond to the enzyme is strong and covalent, inhibition is **irreversible**.

slides.narration: Many drugs work by blocking enzymes. An enzyme holds its usual molecule, the substrate, in a pocket called the active site. A drug with a similar shape can sit in the pocket instead, so the substrate cannot bind and the reaction stops. That is competitive inhibition. Other drugs bind at a different site and change the shape of the pocket, and some form strong bonds that block the enzyme permanently.

slides.heading: Drugs that act on receptors
slides.body_md: **Receptors** are proteins in cell membranes that receive chemical messengers (such as neurotransmitters and hormones) and pass a signal into the cell. **Agonists** mimic the natural messenger and switch the receptor on. **Antagonists** bind to the receptor and block it, preventing the messenger’s action.

slides.narration: Cells talk to each other using chemical messengers. A messenger fits into a receptor protein in the cell membrane, like a key in a lock, and a signal passes into the cell. A drug that copies the messenger and switches the receptor on is an agonist. A drug that sits in the receptor and blocks it is an antagonist, which is useful when a message is being sent too strongly.

slides.heading: Worked example: enzyme or receptor?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Decide whether each drug acts on an enzyme or a receptor, and how: (a) a drug with a shape similar to an enzyme’s substrate that competes for the active site; (b) a drug that blocks histamine from binding at its receptors in the stomach; (c) a drug that copies a natural messenger to trigger its receptor.

**(a)** Enzyme — competitive inhibitor.

**(b)** Receptor — antagonist (e.g. ranitidine-type antacid).

**(c)** Receptor — agonist.

visual.alt: Table of three drugs with their targets and modes of action

slides.narration: Ask what the drug binds to and what it does there. A substrate look-alike that competes for an enzyme’s pocket is a competitive inhibitor. A drug that stops histamine reaching its receptor is a receptor antagonist. A drug that imitates the natural messenger and switches the receptor on is an agonist.

slides.body_md: Identify how a drug interacts with its target.
slides.narration: Quick check. Decide whether the drug blocks a target or imitates the natural messenger.

slides.heading: Antacids and antihistamines
slides.body_md: **Antacids** relieve excess stomach acid: weak bases such as **sodium hydrogencarbonate**, **magnesium hydroxide** and **aluminium hydroxide** neutralise it. Overuse of NaHCO₃ makes the stomach alkaline and triggers more acid. Modern drugs such as **cimetidine** and **ranitidine** block histamine at stomach receptors, so less acid is released. **Antihistamines** (brompheniramine, terfenadine) block histamine at other receptors, relieving allergies such as sneezing and itching.

visual.alt: Table of antacids and antihistamines and how they act

slides.narration: When the stomach produces too much acid, antacids help. Simple antacids, like magnesium hydroxide, are bases that neutralise the acid. Insoluble bases are preferred, because soluble ones can overshoot and make the stomach alkaline, prompting even more acid. Newer drugs stop the acid being released by blocking histamine at stomach receptors. Antihistamines block histamine at other receptors and relieve allergic sneezing and itching.

slides.heading: Worked example: antacid calculation
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A patient has about $0.020\ \text{mol}$ of excess HCl in the stomach. What mass of magnesium hydroxide ($M = 58$) is needed to neutralise it?

**Step 1.** $\ce{Mg(OH)2 + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + 2H2O}$: 1 mol Mg(OH)₂ neutralises 2 mol HCl.

**Step 2.** Moles of Mg(OH)₂ $= 0.020 \div 2 = 0.010$.

**Step 3.** Mass $= 0.010 \times 58 = 0.58\ \text{g}$.

visual.alt: Table of moles of acid, moles of base and mass of magnesium hydroxide

slides.narration: Use the balanced equation. One mole of magnesium hydroxide neutralises two moles of hydrochloric acid. So nought point nought two moles of acid needs nought point nought one moles of the base. Multiplying by the molar mass, fifty eight, gives just over half a gram, which is roughly the amount of base in a typical antacid dose.

slides.heading: Tranquilisers and analgesics
slides.body_md: **Tranquilisers** act on the nervous system to relieve stress and anxiety: e.g. **equanil** (for depression and hypertension), barbiturates such as **veronal** and **seconal** (hypnotics, sleep-producing). **Analgesics** reduce pain without loss of consciousness: **non-narcotic** (aspirin, paracetamol) relieve pain and fever; aspirin also reduces inflammation and prevents blood clotting. **Narcotic** analgesics (morphine, codeine) relieve severe pain but cause sleep and addiction, so they are strictly controlled.

visual.alt: Table of non-narcotic and narcotic analgesics

slides.narration: Tranquilisers calm the nervous system and are used for anxiety and some mental illnesses; some, called hypnotics, help people sleep. Analgesics reduce pain. Non-narcotic ones like aspirin and paracetamol also bring down fever, and aspirin reduces inflammation and thins the blood. Narcotic analgesics like morphine relieve severe pain but are habit-forming, so they are given only under strict medical control.

slides.heading: Antimicrobials: antibiotics
slides.body_md: **Antimicrobials** destroy or prevent the growth of microbes: antibacterials, antifungals, antivirals, antiparasitics. **Antibiotics** are chemicals (originally from micro-organisms) that inhibit or kill microbes. **Bactericidal:** kill bacteria (penicillin, ofloxacin, aminoglycosides). **Bacteriostatic:** stop growth (erythromycin, tetracycline, chloramphenicol). **Broad-spectrum** antibiotics act on many types of bacteria (chloramphenicol, ampicillin, amoxycillin); **narrow-spectrum** on a few (penicillin G). Salvarsan (arsenic-based, for syphilis) and **sulphonamides** (prontosil → sulphanilamide) were early synthetic antimicrobials.

visual.alt: Table classifying antibiotics with examples

slides.narration: Antibiotics are chemicals, first discovered in micro-organisms like moulds, that fight bacterial infections. Some kill bacteria outright and are called bactericidal; others only stop them multiplying, leaving the body’s defences to finish the job, and are called bacteriostatic. A broad-spectrum antibiotic works against many kinds of bacteria; a narrow-spectrum one against a few. Antibiotics must be taken exactly as prescribed, to avoid resistance.

slides.heading: Quick check: medicines
slides.body_md: Classify a medicine by its use or action.
slides.narration: Quick check. Recall which drugs relieve pain, which calm anxiety and which kill bacteria.

slides.heading: Antiseptics, disinfectants and antifertility drugs
slides.body_md: **Antiseptics** kill or prevent growth of micro-organisms on **living tissue** (wounds, skin): Dettol (chloroxylenol + terpineol), bithionol (in soaps), iodine tincture (2–3% iodine in alcohol–water), boric acid (eyes). **Disinfectants** are used on **non-living** objects (floors, drains, instruments). The same substance can be both, depending on **concentration**: 0.2% phenol is an antiseptic, 1% phenol a disinfectant; chlorine at 0.2–0.4 ppm in water is a disinfectant. **Antifertility drugs** are synthetic steroid hormones (progestogen + oestrogen derivatives, e.g. norethindrone, ethynylestradiol).

rows: Chlorine (0.2–0.4 ppm in water), SO₂ (low concentration)

visual.alt: Table contrasting antiseptics and disinfectants with examples

slides.narration: Antiseptics and disinfectants both kill germs, but they are used on different things. Antiseptics, like Dettol or iodine tincture, are gentle enough for skin and wounds. Disinfectants are stronger and are used on floors, drains and instruments. Often the difference is only concentration: a very dilute phenol solution is an antiseptic, while a stronger one is a disinfectant. Antifertility drugs are synthetic steroid hormones used in birth control pills.

slides.heading: Quick check: antiseptic or disinfectant
slides.body_md: Decide whether a substance at a given concentration is an antiseptic or a disinfectant.
slides.narration: Quick check. Ask whether it is meant for living tissue or for non-living objects.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Drugs: small molecules acting on targets; medicines are drugs with a therapeutic effect.
Enzyme inhibitors (competitive, allosteric, irreversible); receptor agonists and antagonists.
Antacids (bases, H₂ blockers); antihistamines; tranquilisers; analgesics (non-narcotic, narcotic).
Antibiotics: bactericidal vs bacteriostatic; broad vs narrow spectrum.
Antiseptics (living tissue) vs disinfectants (non-living); concentration matters.

visual.alt: Summary table of drug classes with examples

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Drugs act mainly on enzymes and receptors, blocking or imitating natural molecules. Medicines are classified by their effect: antacids, antihistamines, tranquilisers, analgesics, antimicrobials and antifertility drugs. Antibiotics may kill bacteria or just stop their growth, and act on a broad or narrow range. Antiseptics are for living tissue, disinfectants for objects.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Give one named example for every class of drug.
Antiseptic vs disinfectant: living vs non-living; same chemical may be both.
Explain why insoluble bases are preferred as antacids.

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: A few tips. Learn one example for each class of medicine. Remember that the same chemical can be an antiseptic or a disinfectant depending on concentration. Keep bactericidal and bacteriostatic straight. And be ready to explain why an insoluble base is a better antacid than baking soda.

decks.title: Chemistry in Everyday Life — Part 2: Chemicals in food
goals: Explain why chemicals are added to food
Describe artificial sweetening agents and compare their sweetness
Describe food preservatives and how they work
Explain the role of antioxidants in food

slides.heading: Chemicals in food
slides.body_md: Part 2 — sweeteners, preservatives and antioxidants.

rows: Sweetness with little or no energy

visual.alt: Table of groups of food additives, their purposes and examples

slides.narration: Look at the label on a packet of biscuits or a bottle of squash and you will find a list of additives. Chemicals are added to food to keep it safe for longer, to make it more appealing, or to change its nutrition. In this part we look at three important groups: artificial sweeteners, preservatives and antioxidants. Additives are allowed only within limits set by food safety laws.

slides.heading: Why add chemicals to food?
slides.body_md: Food additives preserve food, improve its appeal and add nutritive value. They include food colours, flavours and sweeteners, fat emulsifiers and stabilisers, flour improvers, antioxidants, preservatives and nutritional supplements (minerals, vitamins, amino acids). Except for nutritional supplements, they generally have **no nutritive value**.

visual.alt: Flow of the purposes of food additives with examples

slides.narration: Additives serve three broad purposes. Some, like preservatives and antioxidants, keep food safe and fresh for longer. Others, like sweeteners, colours and emulsifiers, make food look, taste or feel better. And some, like added vitamins and minerals, improve nutrition, as in iodised salt. Apart from those nutrients, most additives provide no nourishment themselves.

slides.heading: Artificial sweetening agents
slides.body_md: Sucrose and fructose are natural sweeteners but add **calories**. **Artificial sweeteners** give sweetness with little or no energy, useful for people with diabetes or those controlling weight. Sweetness is compared with cane sugar (sucrose = 1).

rows: Unstable at cooking temperatures; used in cold foods and drinks
Trichloro derivative of sucrose; stable at cooking temperature; no calories
Very potent; sweetness hard to control

visual.alt: Table of artificial sweeteners with sweetness relative to sucrose and notes

slides.narration: Sugar is sweet but full of energy. Artificial sweeteners give the taste of sweetness in tiny amounts, with almost no energy, so they help people with diabetes and those watching their weight. Saccharin is about five hundred and fifty times as sweet as sugar. Aspartame is about a hundred times sweeter but breaks down when heated, so it is used only in cold foods. Sucralose survives cooking.

slides.heading: Worked example: matching sweetness
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A recipe for a cold dessert uses $33\ \text{g}$ of sugar. What mass of saccharin (sweetness 550) would give the same sweetness? Could aspartame be used if the dessert were baked instead?

**Step 1.** Mass of saccharin $= 33 \div 550 = 0.06\ \text{g}$ (60 mg).

**Step 2.** No — aspartame decomposes at cooking temperatures; sucralose, which is heat-stable, could be used for a baked dessert.

headers: Mass for the sweetness of 33 g sugar

visual.alt: Table of masses of sweeteners equivalent in sweetness to thirty three grams of sugar

slides.narration: Because saccharin is five hundred and fifty times as sweet as sugar, we divide the mass of sugar by five hundred and fifty: only about sixty milligrams is needed. If the dessert is to be baked, aspartame is a poor choice because heat destroys it; sucralose, which is stable on heating, would work instead.

slides.heading: Quick check: sweeteners
slides.body_md: Choose a suitable sweetener for a situation.
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about stability on heating and how many times sweeter each sweetener is.

slides.heading: Food preservatives
slides.body_md: **Preservatives** prevent spoilage by microbial growth. Traditional ones: **table salt**, **sugar** and **vegetable oils** (pickles, jams). Common chemical preservatives: **sodium benzoate** (in small amounts; metabolised to hippuric acid and excreted), salts of **sorbic acid** and **propanoic acid**.

rows: Inhibits growth of moulds and bacteria

visual.alt: Table of preservatives, their uses and how they work

slides.narration: Food spoils mainly because bacteria and moulds grow in it. Our grandparents preserved mango pickle with salt and oil, and fruit as jam with lots of sugar: high concentrations of salt or sugar draw water out of microbes by osmosis, so they cannot grow. Factories add small amounts of sodium benzoate to squashes and sauces; the body converts it to hippuric acid and excretes it.

slides.heading: Worked example: preservative concentration
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A food rule allows sodium benzoate up to $0.1\%$ by mass in a fruit squash. What is the maximum mass of sodium benzoate in a $750\ \text{g}$ bottle?

**Step 1.** $0.1\% = 0.1 \div 100 = 0.001$.

**Step 2.** Maximum mass $= 0.001 \times 750 = 0.75\ \text{g}$.

visual.alt: Table of squash mass, limit and maximum mass of preservative

slides.narration: Percentage by mass means grams per hundred grams. Nought point one percent is one thousandth. One thousandth of seven hundred and fifty grams is nought point seven five grams. Food laws set such limits so that preservatives stay at levels that are safe to consume.

slides.heading: Quick check: preservatives
slides.body_md: Explain how a preservative stops food spoiling.
slides.narration: Quick check. Salt and sugar work by osmosis; sodium benzoate inhibits microbial growth.

slides.heading: Antioxidants in food
slides.body_md: Fats and oils react slowly with oxygen and turn **rancid** (bad smell and taste). **Antioxidants** react with oxygen or with free radicals more readily than the food does, so they slow down oxidation. Common food antioxidants: **BHT** (butylated hydroxytoluene) and **BHA** (butylated hydroxyanisole), often with citric or ascorbic acid; **sulfur dioxide** and **sulfites** in wine, beer and fruit juices.

rows: Added with BHA/BHT to boost their effect

visual.alt: Table of food antioxidants and their uses

slides.narration: Leave a packet of fried snacks open for a few weeks and they start to smell stale. Fats and oils react with oxygen in the air, a process called rancidity. Antioxidants protect food by reacting with oxygen or with free radicals faster than the food does. Butylated hydroxy compounds, known as BHA and BHT, are added to butter, oils and snacks, and sulfur dioxide protects fruit juices.

slides.heading: Quick check: antioxidants
slides.body_md: Identify the role of an antioxidant in food.
slides.narration: Quick check. Antioxidants are sacrificed so that the food itself is not oxidised.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Food additives preserve, improve appeal or add nutrients.
Artificial sweeteners: aspartame (100), saccharin (550), sucralose (600), alitame (2000).
Aspartame is unstable on heating; sucralose is heat-stable.
Preservatives: salt, sugar, oil, sodium benzoate, sorbates, propanoates.

visual.alt: Summary table matching food problems to additives

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 2. Food additives keep food safe, make it more appealing, or add nutrients. Artificial sweeteners give sweetness without calories, with very different strengths and heat stabilities. Preservatives stop microbes spoiling food, and antioxidants stop fats going rancid. All are used within legal limits.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: Learn the relative sweetness of the four sweeteners.
State why aspartame is used only in cold foods.
Name sodium benzoate and its fate in the body (hippuric acid).
Give BHA and BHT as antioxidants for fats.

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 2 and their fixes

slides.narration: Final tips. Learn the sweetness numbers and the heat stability of each sweetener. Know how preservatives such as salt, sugar and sodium benzoate work. Do not confuse preservatives, which stop microbes, with antioxidants, which stop oxidation. And name BHA and BHT when asked for antioxidants.

notes.title: Chemistry in Everyday Life — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Drugs and their targets
sections.body_md:
**Drugs:** chemicals of low molecular mass (about 100–500 u) that interact with macromolecular targets to give a biological response. **Medicines:** drugs with a therapeutic effect, used for diagnosis, prevention or treatment; most are harmful in larger doses, so they are used only under medical supervision.

**Classification:** by pharmacological effect (analgesics, antiseptics), by drug action on a biochemical process (antihistamines), by chemical structure (sulphonamides), by molecular target (drugs acting on enzymes, receptors).

**Enzymes as targets:** drugs may block the active site (**competitive inhibitors**), bind at an **allosteric** site to change the active site’s shape, or bind covalently (**irreversible** inhibition).

**Receptors as targets:** membrane proteins that receive chemical messengers. **Agonists** mimic the messenger; **antagonists** block the receptor.

key_terms.definition_md: A low-molecular-mass chemical that interacts with a macromolecular target in the body and produces a biological response.
A drug that competes with the natural substrate for the active site of an enzyme.
A drug that binds to a receptor and blocks the natural messenger without activating it.
A drug that mimics the natural messenger and switches a receptor on.

sections.heading: 2. Therapeutic classes I: antacids, antihistamines, tranquilisers, analgesics
sections.body_md:
- **Antacids:** NaHCO₃, Mg(OH)₂, Al(OH)₃ neutralise excess acid ($\ce{Mg(OH)2 + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + 2H2O}$). Insoluble bases are preferred: excess soluble base makes the stomach alkaline and triggers more acid. **H₂-receptor blockers** (cimetidine, ranitidine) stop histamine from stimulating acid release.
- **Antihistamines:** brompheniramine, terfenadine — block histamine receptors in allergy (they do not affect acid secretion).
- **Tranquilisers:** for stress and mental illness — equanil (depression, hypertension); barbiturates (veronal, amytal, seconal, nembutal) as hypnotics.
- **Analgesics:** relieve pain without impairing consciousness. Non-narcotic: aspirin (also antipyretic, anti-inflammatory, prevents platelet clotting), paracetamol. Narcotic: morphine, codeine (severe pain; sleep and addiction).

key_terms.definition_md: A substance that neutralises excess stomach acid.
A drug acting on the central nervous system to relieve stress, anxiety or mental illness.
A drug that reduces pain without causing loss of consciousness.

sections.heading: 3. Therapeutic classes II: antimicrobials and antifertility drugs
sections.body_md:
**Antimicrobials** destroy or check microbes: antibacterials, antifungals, antivirals, antiparasitics. Early synthetic antimicrobials: **salvarsan** (arsenic compound, for syphilis), **prontosil** (converted in the body to **sulphanilamide**; led to the sulpha drugs).

**Antibiotics:** chemicals (originally from micro-organisms, now also synthesised) that kill or inhibit microbes.
- **Bactericidal** (kill): penicillin, aminoglycosides, ofloxacin. **Bacteriostatic** (stop growth): erythromycin, tetracycline, chloramphenicol.
- **Broad-spectrum** (many bacteria): ampicillin, amoxycillin, chloramphenicol, vancomycin, ofloxacin. **Narrow-spectrum**: penicillin G. **Limited spectrum**: one organism or disease.

**Antiseptics** (living tissue): Dettol (chloroxylenol + terpineol), bithionol, iodine tincture (2–3% I₂ in alcohol–water), iodoform, boric acid (eyes). **Disinfectants** (non-living objects): 1% phenol, chlorine (0.2–0.4 ppm in water), low concentrations of SO₂. 0.2% phenol is an antiseptic.

**Antifertility drugs:** synthetic progesterone derivatives with oestrogen derivatives, e.g. norethindrone, ethynylestradiol (novestrol).

key_terms.definition_md: Describes an antibiotic that kills bacteria.
Describes an antibiotic that stops the growth of bacteria.
An antibiotic effective against a wide range of bacteria.
A chemical applied to living tissue to kill or prevent growth of micro-organisms.
A chemical applied to non-living objects to kill micro-organisms.

sections.heading: 4. Artificial sweetening agents
sections.body_md:
Natural sweeteners (sucrose, fructose) add calories. **Artificial sweeteners** give sweetness with little or no energy — useful for diabetics and for weight control.

| Sweetener | Sweetness (sucrose = 1) | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Aspartame | 100 | Unstable at cooking temperature; cold foods and soft drinks only |
| Saccharin | 550 | First popular sweetener; excreted unchanged in urine |
| Sucralose | 600 | Trichloro derivative of sucrose; heat-stable; no calories |
| Alitame | 2000 | High potency; sweetness hard to control |

Mass needed for equal sweetness $=$ mass of sucrose $\div$ relative sweetness.

key_terms.definition_md: A synthetic chemical that tastes sweet but provides little or no energy.

sections.heading: 5. Food preservatives and antioxidants
sections.body_md:
**Food additives** preserve food, improve appeal or add nutrients (colours, flavours, sweeteners, emulsifiers, flour improvers, antioxidants, preservatives, vitamins and minerals). Apart from nutritional supplements, they have no nutritive value.

**Preservatives** prevent microbial spoilage: table salt, sugar and vegetable oils (traditional); **sodium benzoate** (small amounts; metabolised to hippuric acid and excreted), salts of sorbic acid and propanoic acid.

**Antioxidants** slow oxidation (rancidity) of fats by reacting with oxygen or free radicals more readily than the food: **BHT**, **BHA** (often with ascorbic or citric acid); **SO₂** and sulfites in wines, beers, sugar syrups and dried fruits.

key_terms.definition_md: A substance that prevents spoilage of food by micro-organisms.
A substance that slows the oxidation of food, preventing rancidity.
Spoiling of fats and oils by oxidation, giving unpleasant smell and taste.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Treating antiseptics and disinfectants as different chemicals rather than different uses or concentrations.
- Calling antihistamines antacids (they act on different histamine receptors).
- Mixing up bactericidal and bacteriostatic examples.
- Saying aspartame can be used in baked foods.
- Confusing preservatives (stop microbes) with antioxidants (stop oxidation).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: class of a named drug or additive, one example.
- Explanations (2–3 marks): mode of action (enzyme, receptor), reason for a choice, with an example.
- Calculations: antacid neutralisation, sweetener equivalents, preservative limits.

questions.stem_md: An antacid tablet contains $0.39\ \text{g}$ of aluminium hydroxide, $\ce{Al(OH)3}$ ($M = 78$). How many moles of HCl can it neutralise?

questions.stem_md: For each situation, name the type of antimicrobial chemical and an example: (a) cleaning a small cut on the knee; (b) treating a bacterial throat infection; (c) making well water safe to drink.

(b) An antibiotic, such as amoxycillin or penicillin, taken as prescribed by a doctor. (c) A disinfectant, such as chlorine at about 0.2–0.4 ppm, which kills microbes in water.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What are drugs and medicines? Why should medicines be taken only under medical advice?

(b) Explain how drugs interact with enzymes and receptors.

(c) Describe antacids and antihistamines, explaining why ranitidine was an improvement over simple antacids.

answer.model_answer_md: Drugs are low-molecular-mass chemicals that interact with macromolecular targets and produce a biological response; medicines are drugs with a therapeutic use. Most drugs are harmful in larger doses, so they are taken only as prescribed. A drug can occupy an enzyme’s active site, competing with the substrate (competitive inhibition), or bind at an allosteric site and change the active site’s shape. At receptors, agonists mimic the natural messenger and switch the receptor on, while antagonists block it. Simple antacids such as Mg(OH)₂ and Al(OH)₃ neutralise excess acid; excess NaHCO₃ makes the stomach alkaline and triggers more acid. Ranitidine blocks histamine at stomach receptors, so less acid is released, treating the cause. Antihistamines such as brompheniramine block histamine in allergies.

questions.solution_md: Definitions; enzymes and receptors; antacids and antihistamines.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Classify antibiotics as bactericidal or bacteriostatic, and as broad- or narrow-spectrum, with examples.

(b) Distinguish antiseptics from disinfectants with two examples of each.

(c) Why must a full course of antibiotics be completed?

answer.model_answer_md: Bactericidal antibiotics kill bacteria, e.g. penicillin, aminoglycosides and ofloxacin; bacteriostatic antibiotics stop their growth, e.g. erythromycin, tetracycline and chloramphenicol. Broad-spectrum antibiotics such as ampicillin, amoxycillin and chloramphenicol act on many kinds of bacteria; narrow-spectrum ones such as penicillin G act on a few. Antiseptics are applied to living tissue, e.g. Dettol and tincture of iodine; disinfectants are used on non-living objects, e.g. 1% phenol and chlorine in water. The same substance may be either, depending on concentration. Stopping a course early leaves surviving bacteria that can multiply, causing a relapse, and may become resistant, making the antibiotic less useful.

questions.solution_md: Classes; antiseptic vs disinfectant; resistance.

answer.model_answer_md: Chemicals are added to food to preserve it, improve its appeal and add nutritive value; additives include colours, flavours and sweeteners, emulsifiers and stabilisers, antioxidants, preservatives and nutritional supplements such as vitamins. answer.model_answer_md: (a) Aspartame, about 100 times as sweet as sugar with negligible energy; suitable because the drink is not heated. questions.stem_md:
(a) Distinguish narcotic from non-narcotic analgesics, with examples.

(b) What are tranquilisers? Give two examples and their uses.

(c) Explain why the same chemical, such as phenol, can be an antiseptic or a disinfectant, and name two other antiseptics.

answer.model_answer_md: Analgesics relieve pain without causing loss of consciousness. Non-narcotic analgesics such as aspirin and paracetamol relieve mild pain and fever; aspirin also reduces inflammation and prevents platelet clotting. Narcotic analgesics such as morphine and codeine relieve severe pain, for example after surgery, but cause sleep and addiction, so they are strictly controlled. Tranquilisers act on the central nervous system to relieve stress, anxiety and mental illness; equanil is used for depression and hypertension, and barbiturates such as veronal and seconal are hypnotics. Whether a chemical is an antiseptic or a disinfectant depends on its concentration: 0.2% phenol is mild enough for skin, while 1% phenol is used on floors and drains. Other antiseptics include Dettol and tincture of iodine.

questions.solution_md: Analgesics; tranquilisers; concentration dependence.
